    Decision-Making with Statistics and Data Science in the Age of AIAbstractArtificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as one of the most significant technological disruptors of contemporary society. It is changing almost every aspect of our lives: how we generate and discuss ideas, gather and process information, automate workflows, write code, solve mathematical problems, and ultimately make decisions.
In this talk, I will present some emerging uses of AI in statistics and data science. I will also reflect on trends I am increasingly seeing as the Editor-in-Chief of the R Journal, which publishes research centred on R, one of the most widely used programming languages for statistics and data science. From this perspective, I have witnessed first-hand how AI is changing journal article writing, R package development, peer review, and copy-editing.
I will discuss both the risks and opportunities that AI brings. As a society, we need to recognise and embrace the distinctive value that humans bring to the table, while adapting to new ways of working, reasoning, and making decisions alongside AI.

    A Data-Driven Framework for Quantifying Airspace Risk Across AustraliaAbstractTurning heterogeneous spatial and temporal data into defensible decisions is a challenge across many sectors. The Australian Digital Airspace Characterisation (ADAC) project, led by QUT with Boeing and FlyFreely, shows how a national-scale, data-driven framework can turn billions of observations into transparent, quantitative insights informing operational planning and policy.
ADAC evaluates over 800 billion proximity events across more than 200 billion locations spanning Australia and its coastlines, integrating satellite and terrestrial sources with aeronautical, terrain, obstacle, population and land-use data. Through advanced statistical and probabilistic modelling, it produces continuous, high-resolution estimates rendered as interactive national-scale maps.
The presentation covers ADAC’s methods and decision-support applications: computational architecture for continental-scale modelling, rare-event methods for quantifying uncertainty in sparse-observation environments, and visualisation turning outputs into actionable maps. We illustrate impact through case studies in health logistics, emergency services, and resource operations, and note stakeholder engagement with CASA.

    From Principles to Decisions: An End-to-End GenAI Evaluation FrameworkAbstractGovernment agencies are increasingly adopting Generative AI(GenAI) to improve public services and information dissemination. However, the variable and context-dependent behaviour of large language models makes it difficult to determine whether these systems are safe, reliable and ready for deployment.While Responsible AI principles provide high-level guidance, practical methods for operationalising them remain limited across the public sector.
This work presents a reusable, end-to-end GenAI Evaluation Framework that supports responsible deployment decisions.The framework combines domain-driven scenario design, automated generation of evaluation datasets, and LLM-as-Judge scoring to assess quality, performance and safety across measures including relevance, grounding, clarity, accuracy, tone, confidentiality and toxicity. Using a Census chatbot as a case study, we demonstrate how the framework transforms evaluation from an ad hoc activity into a continuous, structured and evidence-based process. By bridging Responsible AI principles and engineering practice, it provides a scalable approach for assessing GenAI systems and supporting trustworthy deployment decisions across government.

    Artificial Intelligence for Medical Imaging: Enhancing Diagnostic Accuracy Through Deep LearningAbstractMedical image analysis is increasingly benefiting from artificial intelligence (AI), offering opportunities to improve diagnostic accuracy and clinical decision-making. This research investigates deep learning approaches for automated classification of medical X-ray images, focusing on musculoskeletal and chest radiographs.
The study combines transfer learning, feature fusion, and attention-based convolutional neural networks to enhance feature extraction and classification performance. Semi-supervised learning techniques were also explored to address limited labelled data. The proposed frameworks were evaluated on multiple datasets, including abnormality detection in musculoskeletal X-rays and classification of chest X-rays containing COVID-19, pneumonia, tuberculosis, and normal cases.
Results demonstrated high classification accuracy and improved model robustness. Explainable AI techniques were applied to visualise regions influencing model predictions, supporting transparency and clinical trust. The findings demonstrate the potential of AI-assisted diagnostic systems to improve healthcare outcomes and support future clinical implementation.

    Bridging Digital Health Innovation and Data Governance: Lessons from Accessing Statewide Electronic Medical Records for Secondary ResearchAbstractDigital health systems generate vast clinical data, creating opportunities for evidence-based policy, planning, and care. Queensland’s integrated electronic Medical Record (ieMR) system offers a valuable platform for population-scale research and secondary data use. This presentation explores the pathway from data availability to decision-making through a case study of accessing de-identified ieMR data for research. Despite mature infrastructure and established partnerships, approvals took nearly two years due to fragmented ethics governance, lengthy Public Health Act processes, and concerns about data scale. The experience shows that evidence generation depends not only on analytical capability but also on governance, stakeholder trust, and social licence. Beyond legal compliance, researchers must demonstrate public benefit and responsible data stewardship. Streamlined governance, transparent engagement, and trusted access frameworks are essential to bridging the gap between technical capability and practical data use, enabling the full value of health data to support research, policy, and innovation

    Multi-Model Ensemble for Automated Longitudinal Electronic Health Records Summarisation in General PracticeAbstractGeneral practice (GP) clinicians managing multimorbidity face burden from fragmented records. Automated longitudinal EHR summarization is underexplored. This study introduces an AI pipeline to evaluate accuracy, completeness, and utility. We adapted ACSQHC Summary guidelines for GP. The pipeline integrates rule-based extraction with LLM ensembles coordinated by a validation agent enforcing schema constraints. Deployed locally on 2,232 multimorbidity patients from GPs in South West Sydney, two clinicians reviewed 500 for error and utility via adjudication. Single-model ablation variants were benchmarked against metrics. All 2,232 records achieved 99.88% validity. For 1,500 instances: inaccuracy 2.8%, hallucination 9.7%, omission 10.5%. Omission peaked in DIAGNOSES (15.0%), hallucination in CLINICAL SUMMARY (12.1%). Utility rated 4/5 by reviewers. Ensemble designs proved more balanced than single-model variants. Automated EHR summarization in GP is feasible with local LLM ensembles but mitigating omission and hallucination remains a challenge. This study establishes a reproducible framework, demonstrating tangible improvements in multimorbidity care via adapted guidelines.

    Sciget.org: Developing a national Virtual Research Environment for data analyticsAbstractAustralian researchers contend with fragmented AI/ML infrastructure, limited GPU access, incompatible software installations, and no consistent governance for sensitive data.
Here we present the design and first delivery phase of a national Virtual Research Environment (VRE): a portable, containerised platform delivering advanced analytics and AI capabilities. The Sciget.org VRE combines an automated container build system, a federated software distribution network based on CERN Virtual Machine File System (CERN VM-FS) (a web-based, global versioning file system optimised for software distribution), GPU-enabled compute, and a virtual desktop. Privacy-preserving large language models offer in-environment coding support.
A three-tier architecture matches security to data sensitivity: open environments for public datasets and early-career training, application-level ISO 27001-aligned environments for moderately sensitive health data, and a foundation for future Trusted Research Environments. We demonstrate an exemplar VREs for the Australian microscopy and the AI/ML community supporting data science and advanced analytics workflows.

    Advanced Analytics and AI Resources Hub: Enabling Data-Driven Decisions in Health ResearchAbstractIn 2023, the Australian Research Data Commons (ARDC) launched a national digital research infrastructure initiative to strengthen Australia’s capacity for digital health research and translation. As part of this program, an ARDC-ADSN collaboration undertook a comprehensive assessment of current digital health infrastructure, including computing capability, data availability, analytics methods, and accessibility. This work identified critical national research infrastructure (NRI) requirements needed to support advanced health data analytics and informed the design of a national framework.
Building on insights from Phase 1, which engaged researchers, government stakeholders and industry partners, Phase 2 applied a structured, collaborative, co-design methodology to develop a sustainable Resource Hub aligned with national health research priorities and the ARDC Advanced Analytics Reference Architecture. The approach was organised around five thematic areas, each addressing a key component of the digital infrastructure stack.
This presentation will provide an overview of the project and summarise the major findings from this work.

    DevOps Principles as data governance for an Aboriginal legal serviceAbstractLegal-assistance data for an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander organisation must answer to two authorities at once: external accountability to government funders, and the data sovereignty of the community it serves. We present the design of a reproducible, open-source data pipeline that turns a transactional legal case-management system into statutory compliance reports. Our central argument is that computational reproducibility — and the DevOps culture of software engineering it borrows from is not merely an efficiency practice but a form of data governance in its own right.
The pipeline is organised as a climb through levels of abstraction, following the DIKW progression: raw extracts (data) are transformed by business rules into curated records (information), aggregated into statutory measures (knowledge), and used to inform service and funding decisions (wisdom). A machine-readable operational specification acts as a single source of truth — documenting business rules, validating data, and making counting definitions testable rather than aspirational. Version control, automated testing, and continuous documentation operationalise governance decisions directly as code.

    From open-access ocean observations to environmental intelligence: enabling data-driven decisions through Australia’s Integrated Marine Observing SystemAbstractThe Integrated Marine Observing System (IMOS) is Australia’s national ocean observing research infrastructure, delivering sustained, open access observations of the marine environment through the National Collaborative Research Infrastructure Strategy (NCRIS). Over the past two decades, IMOS has generated more than 1.5 billion measurements spanning Australia’s polar, temperate and tropical coastal and oceanic waters, creating a rich evidence base for research, industry and government.
Through the Australian Ocean Data Network (AODN), IMOS provides access to more than 200 quality-controlled marine data collections, near real-time and historical ocean information, cloud-optimised datasets, and open-source Python and R tools that support scalable analytics, visualisation, integration and emerging AI applications.
This talk will showcase how IMOS enables the transition from data to decisions by supporting environmental assessment, policy, and operational decision-making across climate science, oceanography, marine ecosystems, fisheries and coastal resilience. IMOS accelerates discovery, supports data-driven decisions, and unlocks broader societal, environmental and economic benefits.

    Museum Data Science: Collection Data Platform and Catalogues as DataAbstractThis paper introduces “Plexus” the new National Museum of Australia collection data platform. This new data platform operates as part of middleware to support existing and new data and media flows for diverse ends and end-users as “nerve centre” for collection data architecture.
Highlights how the Museum as a domain producer of trusted collection data products and services is moving to an operational model that accords with two of the four data mesh concepts: data ownership and data as a product made available through an API layer for internal and external consumers.
Presents the Australian Institute of Anatomy (AIA) collection card catalogue as a case study. The AIA catalogue demonstrates the value of catalogues “as data” with multiple sources of data and layers of documentation generated by successive collection stewards over time and with multiple access controls.
References recent research “exploring the perspectives of cultural heritage organisations on Collections as Data frameworks internationally.” Hymbel, Nyhan & Pearlman, Perspectives from Germany and Australia, Collections as Data Infrastructure https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003666530-6.

    The Microdata DividendAbstractAt a time when survey response rates are falling globally, the Australian Bureau of Statistics has invested heavily in confidentialised microdata for research. Operated under strict privacy protections and in secure data environments, the Person-Level Integrated Data Asset (PLIDA) and the Business Longitudinal Analytical Data Environment (BLADE) sit alongside other assets such as the Australian Census Longitudinal Dataset, the Longitudinally Linked Employer-Employee Database, the Australian Census and Migrants Integrated Dataset and the Vocational Education and Training National Data Asset.
These datasets allow researchers to follow people and firms over time and study policy effects at scale. They enable randomised trials to track outcomes through administrative records and nonprofits to evaluate client outcomes. Already, linked microdata has informed government policies, including merger reform and the decision to ban non-compete clauses for low- and middle-income workers. This talk looks at what Australia’s expanding microdata infrastructure offers researchers, how these assets are being used by international experts, the role of the APS Data Profession, and where the next gains might come from.

    Predicting Custodial Length of Stay for Women in NSWAbstractWomen in custody experience distinct pathways, needs and offence patterns, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women are overrepresented in custody. This study investigates whether custodial length of stay can be predicted for women entering custody prior to sentencing using offence, legal history and demographic information. The project is a collaboration between the University of Sydney and Corrective Services NSW, in partnership with MobReady, an Aboriginal-owned organisation supporting women around release from custody. Using Corrective Services NSW’s Offender Integrated Management System and the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research Re-offending Database, we compare a variety of regression and machine-learning methods to predict length of stay in custody using information available at reception, when approximately 88% of women are unsentenced. Models are evaluated within a consistent predictive framework, and a simulation study is used to validate feature selection methods. The resulting prediction framework could support evidence-based case management, service planning, and pre- and post-release support for women in custody in NSW.

    A Bayesian Ensemble Projection of Climate Change and Technological Impacts on Future Crop YieldsAbstractThis work introduces a Bayesian hierarchical modeling framework within a fully probabilistic setting for crop yield estimation, model selection, and uncertainty forecasting under multiple future greenhouse gas emission scenarios. By informing on regional agricultural impacts, this approach addresses broader risks to global food security. Extending an established multivariate econometric crop-yield model to incorporate country-specific error variances, the framework systematically relaxes restrictive homogeneity assumptions and enables transparent decomposition of predictive uncertainty into contributions from climate models, emission scenarios, and crop model parameters. In both in-sample and out-of-sample analyses focused on global wheat production, the results demonstrate significant improvements in calibration and probabilistic accuracy of yield projections. These advances provide policymakers and stakeholders with detailed, risk-sensitive information to support the development of more resilient and adaptive agricultural and climate strategies in response to escalating climate-related risks.

    DROVER: a beef-sector CGE for supply-shock decisions, run from an ordinary chatbotAbstractComputable general equilibrium models trace shocks through an economy. We built one for Australia’s beef sector, called DROVER. It models herds, feed, processing, and trade, for livestock stakeholders facing a crisis.
We work through two decisions. First, an animal phase down against a fuel or food supply interruption known in advance. When feed cannot reach animals, some will be lost, and the model helps size and schedule the phase down to preserve breeding stock and downstream processing capacity. The second aims to avoid the phase down entirely. Here the model plans grain importation, sizing port and storage infrastructure against the cost and lead time of building it.
The second thread of the talk is about who can drive the model. This kind of analysis has sat behind a programming barrier that ties the decision-maker to a human modeller. With the Model Context Protocol running in code mode, a user poses scenarios in plain language, revised as questions sharpen, resulting in a policy brief. These tools already sit on every executive’s desktop. In a live session we work from question to brief, then discuss the impact of decision owners manipulating the model themselves.

    Before the Failure: Predictive Fault Detection in Multistage Printhead ManufacturingAbstractMultistage manufacturing processes (MMPs) such as thermal inkjet printhead production accumulate rich measurement data across successive assembly and test operations, yet most quality control remains reactive, identifying defective units only at the final tests. Classical statistical process control (SPC) monitors whether a process remains in control, but does not predict whether an individual unit will fail. This work develops methods for predictive fault detection at the level of the individual unit.
A central challenge is selective labelling: units removed at early stages are not observed at later ones, so the available data reflect only those units that survive, biasing conventional predictive models. We investigate approaches based on stream-of-variation (SoV) modelling, conformal prediction and machine learning techniques to detect incipient faults while providing calibrated, unit-level measure of uncertainty. Using data from an industrial manufacturing execution system, we evaluate these methods against standard baselines and discuss their implications for earlier, more reliable fault detection in high-volume manufacturing.

    Bayesian Adaptive Sampling Design and Decision Support Tools for EcologistsAbstractEcological sampling and research prioritisation strategies tend to be guided by local expertise and individual research programs, rather than optimised against explicit, quantitative objectives. A broad family of Bayesian adaptive design methods has the potential to add value across ecological sampling contexts, but remains underutilised. Paired with accessible decision support tools, these methods offer evidence-based approaches to recurring allocation problems in ecology: deciding where and what to sample, which specimens to prioritise for digitisation from collection backlogs, or where to triage conservation information-gathering given national biodiversity priorities.
We map the landscape of Bayesian adaptive design methods, distinguishing approaches by goal and utility function - including Value of Information methods, information-theoretic approaches targeting model improvement, and sequential allocation for yield maximisation. Worked examples illustrate practical applications, including expected information gain for wombat sampling design, Rényi entropy search for African lovegrass distribution modelling, and species discovery in Australian weevils using bandit algorithms.

    Spatial Conservation Prioritisation for Matters of National Environmental SignificanceAbstractAs an authoritative source for national information about Australia’s environment, Environment Information Australia (EIA) publishes geospatial data on where nationally threatened species habitat is likely to occur and how many unique species are predicted to occur in a specific area. This information is used to guide planning and prioritisation of government investment in protection, conservation, and restoration of threatened species and their habitat. Spatial conservation prioritisation (SCPr) integrates the spatial distribution of species with other biodiversity data to produce national-scale prioritisation products. EIA is applying SCPr across multiple use cases including the recently published Relative habitat importance for threatened and migratory species dataset to identify high-priority areas across Australia for nationally threatened biodiversity, offering a consistent and reproducible evidence base to support environmental decision-making. These analyses complement existing regulatory frameworks by providing spatial tools that can inform strategic planning and investment prioritisation in an evolving policy landscape to protect Australia’s most threatened biodiversity.

    From satellite data to preventative decisions: operationalising remote sensing to reduce sediment pollution risk from urban developmentAbstractConstruction-related earthworks are a persistent source of sediment pollution in urban growth areas, particularly when site preparation and bulk earthworks expose large areas of bare soil on site without appropriate preventative control measures. Regulatory responses are often triggered after environmental harm has occurred. Prevention capabilities are limited by currently available information.
This presentation describes how EPA Victoria and University of Melbourne combined satellite imagery, geospatial analytics and environmental science into an operational decision-support capability for proactive, preventative risk-based regulation.
The project developed and evaluated a passive, large-scale monitoring system for detecting land disturbance and earthworks at greenfield development sites. The system uses freely available Sentinel-2 imagery and automated analysis of spectral indices to detect bulk earthworks and site preparation activities.
The system provides a practical pathway for EPA Victoria decision makers to prioritise inspections, engage duty holders, share intelligence with local government and other partners, and improve erosion and sediment control outcomes.

    A Bayesian Multi-Stage Ensemble for Detecting Bats and Raptors from Radar DataAbstractWind turbine developments in remote arid environments require reliable monitoring of aerial fauna to manage collision risk. Robin Radar systems deployed in the Pilbara region track thousands of airborne objects, but their onboard classifier distinguishes targets mainly by body size, giving limited species-level information. Estimating species-specific collision probability, essential for impact assessment and compliance, depends on resolving this identification gap.
This study presents a multi-paradigm ML framework converting radar tracks into species-level classifications. Preprocessing removes clutter and non-biological detections, corrects airspeeds using wind profiles, and adjusts for detection bias. A Bayesian Ensemble integrates unsupervised clustering of body signatures, semi-supervised self-training on flight kinematics, and supervised discriminant analysis of track context, fusing posteriors via Bayesian log-odds with retained uncertainty.
The framework identifies micro-bats, ghost bats, and wedge-tailed eagles from nocturnal and diurnal tracks, flagging conflicting detections for review and enabling species-level collision-risk assessment in arid landscapes.

title: Code of Conduct
text:
The organisers of the Australian Data Science Network Conference 2026 are committed to providing a conference that is welcoming and safe for all participants, is free from unlawful discrimination and harassment, and where all participants are treated with dignity and respect. Harassment is unlawful under both federal and all Australian state anti-discrimination laws, and as such, people suspected of such misconduct may be reported to authorities. Adherence to this Code of Conduct is a requirement for all conference participants and sponsors, and covers all aspects of this conference, including conference sessions and breaks, all social events and all communication, including that via email or social media (including but not limited to Facebook and X (formerly Twitter)) associated with the conference. Unacceptable behaviour includes, but is not limited to:
To report violations of this Code of Conduct, alert a member of the Response Team (names and contact details listed below). Reports may be made by people subject to, or witnesses of, unacceptable behaviour.

title: Code of Conduct
text:
Code of Conduct Response Team
[In this section list the names, email addresses, and if appropriate, telephone numbers, of people tasked with responding to reports of violations of the Code. At least two people must be listed, but ideally there will be several listed contacts, from a variety of institutions/workplaces, including both men and women. The list should include, but is not limited to, conference/meeting organisers. Ideally members of this response team will have some training in dealing with reports of harassment.]
For example: Abba B Abbason, Senior Lecturer at Stats University. Email:…, Phone number:….
If an individual participates in unacceptable behaviour, the Response Team may take lawful action that they deem appropriate, including asking the individual to stop or removal of the individual from the [conference/event/meeting] without refund of registration and/or other applicable fees. Reports of unacceptable behaviour may be communicated to the Statistical Society of Australia, and individuals who participate in unacceptable behaviour may face consequences including being disallowed from attending future events. Individuals who are ejected will not be allowed to give any planned oral or poster presentations, and their place may be allocated to another attendee. The reason for the replacement presentation may also be announced (e.g., “Professor X has violated this event’s code of conduct and has been asked to leave and therefore will not be able to present today, in their place we will instead hear from …”). Violations may be reported to the individual’s employer or research funders. Statistical Society of Australia members may have their membership cancelled without refund of membership fees.
All efforts will be made to protect the anonymity of persons reporting violations. Persons reporting violations of the Code may request that their report remain confidential and that no further action be taken. However, if the Code of Conduct Response Team deems it necessary for the safety of event attendees, action will be taken, including referral of the report to the Statistical Society of Australia. This Code of Conduct is designed to ensure that this event can be enjoyed by all participants.
We hope you have an inspiring and enjoyable time.

title: Modern Data Linkage Methods and Implementation Using Splink
text:
Linked data assets, such as the Person Level Integrated Data Asset (PLIDA), are a rich source of information, allowing the analysis of interconnected systems such as healthcare, government services, education, and taxation. But the creation of these assets is not always straightforward, as often there is not a deterministic way of identifying individuals across datasets, such as with a unique identifier. Probabilistic data linkage methods can help resolve this problem by comparing fields common across datasets and give an estimate of how likely two records belong to the same individual.
This one-day pre-conference workshop on probabilistic linking using the Python package Splink will cover:
The workshop will be presented by Aymon Wuolanne and Daniel Fearnley, from the Data Linking Methodology section in the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS). They work on the development and productionisation of Splink at the ABS, which is used to produce data assets like PLIDA.
No prior background in probabilistic linking theory is required, although a basic understanding of Python is recommended.
This workshop is open to everyone, not just conference delegates.

title: Modern Data Linkage Methods and Implementation Using Splink
text:
Presenters

Daniel Fearnley


Daniel joined the ABS in 2011, and has spent the last 3 years in Data Linking Methodology where he has led the team responsible for assessing the feasibility of the probabilistic linkage tool Splink, and the transition to using Splink as the default linking tool for all ABS person-level linkages. His team won the 2026 APS Data Award in Data System and Innovation for their work on Splink. Outside of work, Daniel enjoys cooking and running (because he likes cooking) and earlier this year he and his wife watched every game of the FIFA World Cup.








Aymon Wuolanne


Aymon joined the ABS as a graduate in 2022 and is currently a methodologist in Data Linking Methodology. In 2025 he won the Ken Foreman Award for his work on building the Person Linkage Spine using Splink, and was a member of the team that won the 2026 APS Data Award in Data System and Innovation for their work on Splink. Outside of work, Aymon enjoys walking, reading, video games and running much slower than Daniel.

title: Conference Program
text:
Keynotes

Dr Emi Tanaka, Australian National University


Emi Tanaka is a statistician, the Australian National University lead for the Analytics for The Australian Grains Industry Project, and Editor-in-Chief of the R Journal. She has a passion for data science and open-source software, which is evident across her work spanning experimental design, mixed-effects models, data visualisation, emerging analytics (machine/deep learning and large language models) and developing better statistical workflows, practice and tools.
Since completing her PhD in statistics in 2015, Emi has been recognised as an expert and leader in her field, delivering numerous invited talks both nationally and internationally and being awarded the Statistical Society of Australia President’s Award for Leadership in Statistics.







Decision-Making with Statistics and Data Science in the Age of AI
Artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as one of the most significant technological disruptors of contemporary society. It is changing almost every aspect of our lives: how we generate and discuss ideas, gather and process information, automate workflows, write code, solve mathematical problems, and ultimately make decisions.
In this talk, I will present some emerging uses of AI in statistics and data science. I will also reflect on trends I am increasingly seeing as the Editor-in-Chief of the R Journal, which publishes research centred on R, one of the most widely used programming languages for statistics and data science. From this perspective, I have witnessed first-hand how AI is changing journal article writing, R package development, peer review, and copy-editing.
I will discuss both the risks and opportunities that AI brings. As a society, we need to recognise and embrace the distinctive value that humans bring to the table, while adapting to new ways of working, reasoning, and making decisions alongside AI.
 



Andrew Leigh MP


Andrew Leigh is the Assistant Minister for Productivity, Competition, Charities and Treasury, and Federal Member for Fenner in the ACT. Prior to being elected in 2010, Andrew was a professor of economics at the Australian National University.
He holds a PhD in Public Policy from Harvard, having graduated from the University of Sydney with first class honours in Arts and Law. Andrew is a past recipient of the Economic Society of Australia’s Young Economist Award and a Fellow of the Australian Academy of Social Sciences.







The Microdata Dividend
At a time when survey response rates are falling globally, the Australian Bureau of Statistics has invested heavily in confidentialised microdata for research. Operated under strict privacy protections and in secure data environments, the Person-Level Integrated Data Asset (PLIDA) and the Business Longitudinal Analytical Data Environment (BLADE) sit alongside other assets such as the Australian Census Longitudinal Dataset, the Longitudinally Linked Employer-Employee Database, the Australian Census and Migrants Integrated Dataset and the Vocational Education and Training National Data Asset.
These datasets allow researchers to follow people and firms over time and study policy effects at scale. They enable randomised trials to track outcomes through administrative records and nonprofits to evaluate client outcomes. Already, linked microdata has informed government policies, including merger reform and the decision to ban non-compete clauses for low- and middle-income workers. This talk looks at what Australia’s expanding microdata infrastructure offers researchers, how these assets are being used by international experts, the role of the APS Data Profession, and where the next gains might come from.
